questions.q: Point charges of \(2.0\ \mu\text{C}\) and \(3.0\ \mu\text{C}\) are 0.30 m apart in air. What is the force between them? (\(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} = 8.99 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{C}^{-2}\))
questions.solution: \(F = \frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{2}} = \frac{8.99 \times 10^{9} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 3.0 \times 10^{-6}}{0.30^{2}}\) = 0.60 N. Forgetting to square the distance (0.18 N) is the usual slip.

questions.q: A charge of \(2.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{C}\) experiences a force of \(4.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{N}\) in an electric field. What is the electric field strength?
questions.solution: Electric field strength is force per unit positive charge: \(E = \frac{F}{Q} = \frac{4.0 \times 10^{-3}}{2.0 \times 10^{-6}} = 2.0 \times 10^{3}\ \text{N C}^{-1}\).

questions.q: Two parallel plates are 0.020 m apart with a potential difference of 600 V between them. What is the electric field strength between the plates?
questions.solution: The field between parallel plates is uniform: \(E = \frac{V}{d} = \frac{600}{0.020} = 3.0 \times 10^{4}\ \text{V m}^{-1}\). Multiplying instead of dividing (12) is the usual slip.

questions.q: The distance from a point charge is doubled. What happens to the electric field strength?
questions.solution: The field of a point charge is radial and follows an inverse square law: \(E = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{2}}\). Doubling the distance divides the field strength by two squared, so it falls to a quarter.

questions.q: What is the electric potential 0.10 m from a point charge of \(1.0 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{C}\)? (\(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} = 8.99 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{C}^{-2}\))
questions.solution: \(V = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r} = \frac{8.99 \times 10^{9} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-9}}{0.10}\) = 90 V. The distance is not squared for potential: squaring it (900) gives the field strength instead.

questions.q: A charge of \(2.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{C}\) is moved through a potential difference of 500 V. How much work is done?
questions.solution: Work done is charge times change in potential: \(\Delta W = Q\Delta V = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 500 = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{J}\).

questions.q: An electron enters a uniform electric field, moving at right angles to the field lines. What is the shape of its path in the field?
questions.solution: The force on the electron is constant in size and direction, so it has a constant acceleration across the field while its velocity along its original direction stays constant. This is the same as a projectile under gravity: the path is a parabola. A circle is the path in a magnetic field.

questions.q: How are equipotential surfaces related to electric field lines?

options.A: They run parallel to the field lines.
options.B: They cross the field lines at 45°.
options.C: They are the same as the field lines.
options.D: They are always at right angles to the field lines.

questions.solution: No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential, so there can be no component of the field along it. Equipotentials are therefore always perpendicular to field lines: spheres around a point charge, and planes parallel to the plates in a uniform field.

questions.q: A capacitor stores a charge of \(6.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{C}\) when the potential difference across it is 12 V. What is its capacitance?
questions.solution: Capacitance is charge stored per unit potential difference: \(C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{6.0 \times 10^{-4}}{12} = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{F}\), which is \(50\ \mu\text{F}\).

questions.q: A \(100\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor is charged to 12 V. How much energy does it store?
questions.solution: \(E = \frac{1}{2}CV^{2} = \frac{1}{2} \times 100 \times 10^{-6} \times 12^{2} = 7.2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{J}\). Forgetting the half, or forgetting to square the potential difference, gives the other values.

questions.q: The separation of the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is doubled, with nothing else changed. What happens to its capacitance?
questions.solution: \(C = \frac{A\varepsilon_{0}\varepsilon_{r}}{d}\), so capacitance is inversely proportional to the separation of the plates. Doubling the separation halves the capacitance.

questions.q: A dielectric is placed between the plates of a capacitor. What effect does it have, and why?

options.A: It lowers the capacitance, because it stops charge flowing between the plates.
options.B: It lowers the capacitance, because its molecules absorb charge from the plates.
options.C: It has no effect, because it is an insulator.
options.D: It raises the capacitance, because its polarised molecules reduce the field between the plates.

questions.solution: The field between the plates makes the polar molecules of the dielectric rotate to line up with it. Their own field opposes the applied field, so the potential difference needed for a given charge is smaller. More charge is stored per volt: the capacitance is larger.

questions.q: A \(100\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor discharges through a \(10\ \text{k}\Omega\) resistor. What is the time constant of the circuit?
questions.solution: Time constant = \(RC = 10 \times 10^{3} \times 100 \times 10^{-6}\) = 1.0 s. Both prefixes must be converted: leaving the resistance in kilohms or the capacitance in microfarads gives the wrong power of ten.

questions.q: A capacitor discharges through a resistor. What percentage of its initial charge remains after one time constant?
questions.solution: \(Q = Q_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}\). After one time constant, \(t = RC\), so the fraction left is \(e^{-1}\) = 0.37, which is 37%. The 63% is the fraction that has gone.

questions.q: A capacitor charged to 12 V discharges through a resistor. The time constant of the circuit is 5.0 s. What is the potential difference across the capacitor after 10 s?
questions.solution: \(V = V_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}\), and 10 s is two time constants. So \(V = 12e^{-2}\) = 1.6 V. After only one time constant it would be 4.4 V.

questions.q: A capacitor is charged from a battery through a resistor. Which describes the graph of current against time?

options.B: It stays constant, then drops to zero.
options.C: It rises quickly at first, then levels off at a maximum.
options.D: It starts at a maximum and falls exponentially towards zero.

questions.solution: At first the capacitor is uncharged, so the full battery voltage is across the resistor and the current is at its largest. As charge builds up, the voltage across the capacitor rises, leaving less across the resistor, so the current decays exponentially. The charge and voltage graphs are the ones that rise and level off.
